L6@P0: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE WEEKLY CLAIMS
L7@P0: SEASONALLY ADJUSTED DATA
L8@P0: In the week ending October 31, the advance figure for seasonally adjusted initial claims was 189,000, a decrease of
L9@P0: 6,000 from the previous week's revised level. The previous week's level was revised up by 1,000 from 194,000 to
L10@P0: 195,000. The 4-week moving average was 194,750, a decrease of 2,250 from the previous week's revised average. The
L11@P0: previous week's average was revised up by 250 from 196,750 to 197,000.
L12@P0: The advance seasonally adjusted insured unemployment rate was 1.1 percent for the week ending October 24,
L13@P0: unchanged from the previous week's unrevised rate. The advance number for seasonally adjusted insured
L14@P0: unemployment during the week ending October 24 was 1,718,000, an increase of 23,000 from the previous week's
L15@P0: revised level. The previous week's level was revised down by 6,000 from 1,701,000 to 1,695,000. The 4-week moving
L16@P0: average was 1,709,500, an increase of 1,000 from the previous week's revised average. The previous week's average was
L17@P0-1: revised down by 1,500 from 1,710,000 to 1,708,500. 2
L18@P1: UNADJUSTED DATA
L19@P1: The advance number of actual initial claims under state programs, unadjusted, totaled 176,698 in the week ending
L20@P1: October 31, a decrease of 2,951 (or -1.6 percent) from the previous week. The seasonal factors had expected an increase
L21@P1: of 2,539 (or 1.4 percent) from the previous week. There were 216,026 initial claims in the comparable week in 2025.
L22@P1: The advance unadjusted insured unemployment rate was 1.0 percent during the week ending October 24, unchanged
L23@P1: from the prior week. The advance unadjusted level of insured unemployment in state programs totaled 1,494,812, an
L24@P1: increase of 10,189 (or 0.7 percent) from the preceding week. The seasonal factors had expected a decrease of 10,169
L25@P1: (or -0.7 percent) from the previous week. A year earlier the rate was 1.1 percent and the volume was 1,712,402.
L26@P1: The total number of continued weeks claimed for benefits in all programs for the week ending October 17 was
L27@P1: 1,507,702, an increase of 8,510 from the previous week. There were 1,756,507 weekly claims filed for benefits in all
L28@P1: programs in the comparable week in 2025.
L29@P1: No state was triggered "on" the Extended Benefits program during the week ending October 17.
L30@P1: Initial claims for UI benefits filed by former Federal civilian employees totaled 552 in the week ending October 24, an
L31@P1: increase of 110 from the prior week. There were 347 initial claims filed by newly discharged veterans, a decrease of 40
L32@P1: from the preceding week.
L33@P1: There were 5,128 continued weeks claimed filed by former Federal civilian employees the week ending October 17, an
L34@P1: increase of 194 from the previous week. Newly discharged veterans claiming benefits totaled 4,941, a decrease of 34
L35@P1-2: from the prior week. 3
L36@P2: The highest insured unemployment rates in the week ending October 17 were in New Jersey (2.0), Washington (1.8),
L37@P2: California (1.7), Massachusetts (1.7), Puerto Rico (1.6), Nevada (1.5), Oregon (1.5), Rhode Island (1.5), New York (1.4),
L38@P2: and Illinois (1.3).
L39@P2: The largest increases in initial claims for the week ending October 24 were in New York (+2,609), Texas (+1,564),
L40@P2: California (+1,043), Pennsylvania (+818), and Ohio (+784), while the largest decreases were in Michigan (-1,813),
L41@P2-3: Tennessee (-977), South Carolina (-763), Kentucky (-496), and Oklahoma (-227). 4

Arm delivers a record second quarter, reaching $1.44 billion in total revenue - Arm Newsroom (https://newsroom.arm.com/news/arm-q2-fye27-results)

L0: News November 4, 2026
L1: # Arm delivers a record second quarter, reaching $1.44 billion in total revenue
L2: 
L3: Arm Q2 FYE27 quarterly earnings mark fifth consecutive quarter of total revenue growth exceeding 20% year over year.
L4: 
L5: Share
L6: 
L7: 【0†Image】
L8: 
L9: Today (November 4, 2026), Arm (NASDAQ: ARM) published a letter to its shareholders containing the company’s results for its second quarter of fiscal year 2027, which ended September 30, 2026. The infographic below provides the key highlights for the quarter:
L10: 【1†Image: Arm Q2 FYE27 financial results infographic showing record total revenue of $1.44 billion, up 27% year-over-year. Licensing revenue reached $773 million, royalty revenue $670 million, GAAP operating income $201 million, and non-GAAP operating income $638 million. CEO Rene Haas highlights strong AI-driven demand and growth in Arm’s compute platform.】
L11: 
L12: Here are what the results mean and how they were achieved:
L13:   * Total revenue for Arm in Q2 FYE27 increased 27% year over year to $1.44 billion, representing Arm’s highest ever second quarter. This reflects strong execution and growing demand for the Arm compute platform.
L14:   * Record second quarter was driven by strong licensing and other revenue of $773 million, reflecting a 50% year over year increase, an important leading indicator of future royalty growth. Meanwhile, royalty revenue for the quarter reached $670 million, with data center royalties doubling year over year.
L15:   * For the first time, Arm’s partners reported more than 10 billion Arm-based chips shipped during the quarter – an increase of 1.5 billion chips year over year – adding to the scale of the platform already used by more than 30 million developers.
L16:   * Arm’s business is driven by two areas – both built on the same Arm compute platform, leveraging a common software ecosystem – that are seeing rapid growth as AI increases the amount and complexity of compute required across every market:
L17:     * The IP business, where partners are increasing investment in Arm technology and deploying record numbers of Arm-based silicon; and
L18:     * The new silicon business, where demand for the 【2†Arm AGI CPU】 is extremely strong.
L19:   * Arm AGI CPU expands the business opportunity by delivering Arm-design silicon directly to customers, with demand continuing to strengthen:
L20:     * Arm’s confidence in achieving up to $2 billion in Arm AGI CPU revenue over FYE27 and FYE28 has increased over the past 90 days, supported by additional supply and customer mix.
L21:     * Purchase orders for Arm AGI CPU have been secured from multiple customers extending through calendar 2027, and the first commercial deliveries are on track for Q4 FYE27.
L22:     * 【3†Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) announced】 plans to offer Arm AGI CPU instances in 2027.
L23:     * 【4†Independent testing by Signal65 showed Arm AGI CPU】 delivering approximately 2x the performance per rack versus AMD EPYC 9755.
L24:   * Arm-based server market share at the top hyperscalers more than tripled – from 15% in calendar 2024 to more than 50% in calendar 2025. Based on current ramps across AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt, and NVIDIA platforms, Arm expects that share to exceed 60% by the end of calendar 2026:
L25:     * Amazon recently reported that Arm-based Graviton revenue commitments increased more than 20x year-over-year.
L26:     * Google identified Arm-based Axion as a critical component of its AI infrastructure.
L27:     * Microsoft highlighted strong adoption of Arm-based Cobalt CPUs.
L28:     * NVIDIA continues to expand its Arm-based Vera CPU platform for agentic AI, with it now generally available on OCI and deployed in production with OpenAI.
L29:   * Arm introduced 【5†Arm Neoverse CSS N4】, enabling partners to develop differentiated silicon CPUs, networking, infrastructure management, and security, and delivering up to 2x performance per socket and 25% better performance per watt than the prior generation.
L30:   * Arm compute sits on both sides of the trust boundary for agentic AI, with NVIDIA’s recently announced OpenShell architecture using Arm-based CPUs to execute AI workloads, and Arm-based BlueField-4 DPUs to independently enforce security and isolation.
L31:   * Arm-based PCs have now reached approximately 20% of global PC shipments, reflecting the 【6†growing adoption of Arm in personal computing】.
L32:     * A new portfolio of PCs powered by 【7†NVIDIA’s Arm-based RTX Spark】 further expands Arm’s reach into local AI, content creation, and gaming for PC.
L33:     * Google introduced Googlebook, a new category of AI-native laptops designed for Gemini Intelligence, with Arm serving as a primary compute platform for many models.
L34:   * In smartphones, 【8†Arm CSS for Mobile 2】 drives the performance of agentic AI workloads up by 70% through 【9†Arm Scalable Matrix Extension 2 (SME2)†www.arm.com】, which is already adopted by major smartphone vendors like OPPO and vivo. Meanwhile, 【10†Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX】, Arm’s first AI-native GPU, delivers up to 4x the frame rate at the same sustained power, with Xiaomi adopting the technology, and leading game developers and engines integrating 【11†Arm Neural Technology†www.arm.com】.

L183:                                                 PRODUCTIVITY AND COSTS
L184:                                             Third Quarter 2026, Preliminary
L185: 
L186:     Nonfarm business sector labor productivity increased 3.6 percent in the third quarter of 2026, the
L187:     U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today, as output increased 3.7 percent and hours worked
L188:     increased 0.1 percent. (All quarterly percent changes in this release are seasonally adjusted annualized
L189:     rates.) From the same quarter a year ago, nonfarm business sector labor productivity increased 2.1
L190:     percent in the third quarter of 2026. (See table A1.)
L191: 
L192:     Unit labor costs in the nonfarm business sector decreased 0.7 percent in the third quarter of 2026,
L193:     reflecting a 2.9-percent increase in hourly compensation and a 3.6-percent increase in productivity. Unit
L194:     labor costs increased 2.4 percent over the last four quarters. (See tables A1 and 2.)
L195:     BLS calculates unit labor costs as the ratio of hourly compensation to labor productivity. Increases in
L196:     hourly compensation tend to increase unit labor costs and increases in productivity tend to reduce them.
L197: 
L198:     =============================================================================================================
L199:                                                 Historical Revisions
L200:     Data in this release reflect the 2026 Annual Update of the National Income and Product Accounts
L201:     (NIPA) released by the Bureau of Economic Analysis of the U.S. Department of Commerce on
L202:     September 30, 2026. See �Revised measures� section.
L203:     =============================================================================================================
L204: 
L205:     Real hourly compensation, which takes into account consumer prices, increased 1.1 percent in the third
L206:     quarter of 2026, and increased 1.0 percent over the last four quarters. The labor share, which is the
L207:     percentage of output that accrues to workers in the form of compensation, was 53.0 percent in the third
L208:     quarter of 2026, the lowest level in the series, which begins in the first quarter of 1947.
L209: 
L210:     Labor productivity, or output per hour, is calculated by dividing an index of real output by an index of
L211:     hours worked by all workers, including employees, proprietors, and unpaid family workers. During the
L212:     current business cycle, starting in the fourth quarter of 2019, labor productivity has grown at an
L213:     annualized rate of 2.2 percent through the third quarter of 2026, reflecting a 2.7-percent rate of growth in
L214:     output and a 0.4-percent rate of growth in hours worked. The 2.2-percent annualized rate of nonfarm
L215:     business productivity growth in the current business cycle thus far is higher than the 1.5-percent rate of
L216:     the previous business cycle, from the fourth quarter of 2007 through the fourth quarter of 2019, and the
L217:     same as the long-term rate of 2.2 percent since the first quarter of 1947.
L218: 
L219:     Manufacturing sector labor productivity increased 0.3 percent in the third quarter of 2026, as output
L220:     increased 1.3 percent and hours worked increased 1.0 percent. In the durable manufacturing sector,
L221:     productivity increased 2.2 percent, reflecting a 3.8-percent increase in output and a 1.6-percent increase
L222:     in hours worked. Nondurable manufacturing sector productivity decreased 1.7 percent, as output
L223:     decreased 1.6 percent and hours worked increased 0.1 percent. Total manufacturing sector productivity
L224:     increased 0.4 percent from the same quarter a year ago. (See tables A1, 3, 4, and 5.)
L225:     Unit labor costs in the total manufacturing sector increased 2.7 percent in the third quarter of 2026, as
L226:     hourly compensation increased 3.0 percent and labor productivity increased 0.3 percent. Manufacturing
L227:     sector unit labor costs increased 4.0 percent from the same quarter a year ago. (See tables A1 and 3.)
L228: 
L229:     The concepts, sources, and methods used for the manufacturing output series differ from those used in
L230:     the business and nonfarm business output series; these output measures are not directly comparable. See
L231:     the Technical Notes for a more detailed explanation.
